Advanced Machine Learning: EasyVisa (Visa Application Processing)¶

Description¶

Context¶

Business communities in the United States are facing high demand for human resources, but one of the constant challenges is identifying and attracting the right talent, which is perhaps the most important element in remaining competitive. Companies in the United States look for hard-working, talented, and qualified individuals both locally as well as abroad.

The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) of the US permits foreign workers to come to the United States to work on either a temporary or permanent basis. The act also protects US workers against adverse impacts on their wages or working conditions by ensuring US employers' compliance with statutory requirements when they hire foreign workers to fill workforce shortages. The immigration programs are administered by the Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC).

OFLC processes job certification applications for employers seeking to bring foreign workers into the United States and grants certifications in those cases where employers can demonstrate that there are not sufficient US workers available to perform the work at wages that meet or exceed the wage paid for the occupation in the area of intended employment.

Objective¶

In FY 2016, the OFLC processed 775,979 employer applications for 1,699,957 positions for temporary and permanent labor certifications. This was a nine percent increase in the overall number of processed applications from the previous year. The process of reviewing every case is becoming a tedious task as the number of applicants is increasing every year.

The increasing number of applicants every year calls for a Machine Learning based solution that can help in shortlisting the candidates having higher chances of VISA approval. OFLC has hired the firm EasyVisa for data-driven solutions. You as a data scientist at EasyVisa have to analyze the data provided and, with the help of a classification model:

Facilitate the process of visa approvals. Recommend a suitable profile for the applicants for whom the visa should be certified or denied based on the drivers that significantly influence the case status.

Data Dictionary¶

The data contains the different attributes of the employee and the employer. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

  • case_id - ID of each visa application
  • continent - Information of continent the employee
  • education_of_employee - Information of education of the employee
  • has_job_experience - Does the employee has any job experience? Y= Yes; N = No
  • requires_job_training - Does the employee require any job training? Y = Yes; N = No
  • no_of_employees - Number of employees in the employer's company
  • yr_of_estab - Year in which the employer's company was established
  • region_of_employment - Information of foreign worker's intended region of employment in the US.
  • prevailing_wage - Average wage paid to similarly employed workers in a specific occupation in the area of intended employment. The purpose of the prevailing wage is to ensure that the foreign worker is not underpaid compared to other workers offering the same or similar service in the same area of employment.
  • unit_of_wage - Unit of prevailing wage. Values include Hourly, Weekly, Monthly, and Yearly.
  • full_time_position - Is the position of work full-time? Y = Full-Time Position; N = Part-Time Position
  • case_status - Flag indicating if the Visa was certified or denied

Observation¶

  • Demographic Profile - Certified approvals skew heavily toward Asian nationals with Bachelor's degrees, prior work experience, and no job training requirements (6 continents, 4 education levels total).
  • Role & Location - Applications concentrate primarily on full-time positions located in the U.S. Northeast (spanning 5 unique U.S. regions).
  • Compensation Variance - prevailing_wage shows extreme dispersion ($\mu \approx \$74\text{k}$, $\sigma \approx \$52\text{k}$, range: $\$2.13$ to $\$319,210$), driven by role disparities and mixed timeframes (hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, annual), though annual (year) is most common.
  • Employer Age - Company founding years range from 1800 to 2016 (median: 1997), representing a mix of legacy and modern firms.
  • Data Quality Issues - no_of_employees contains severe anomalies requiring cleaning, including negative values ($-26$) and massive outliers ($602,069$).
  • Binary Variables - has_job_experience, requires_job_training, and full_time_position serve as standard boolean indicators.

Univariate Analysis¶

Numerical (continuous) variables and histogram¶

In [17]:
# define the plot figure size
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 7))

# define the list of continuous numerical features to plot histogram to analyse the distribution and its skewness
numerical_features = ['no_of_employees', 'prevailing_wage', 'yr_of_estab']

# plot the histogram for each numerical feature
for i, feature in enumerate(numerical_features):
    plt.subplot(3, 1, i+1)
    sns.histplot(data[feature], kde=True)
    plt.title(f'Distribution of {feature}')
    plt.xlabel

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations¶

  • Employee Count Distribution - no_of_employees exhibits strong right-skewness, reflecting a ecosystem dominated by small-to-midsize enterprises with a long right tail of massive corporate outliers.
  • Compensation Distribution - prevailing_wage is right-skewed, with the majority of roles clustering at lower salary baselines and a high-earning tail extending into the $\$150\text{k}$–$\$300\text{k}$ range.
  • Employer Age Distribution - yr_of_estab displays pronounced left-skewness, showing a heavy concentration of recently established firms along with a sparse tail of legacy companies founded prior to 1950 and 1850.

Observations¶

  • Geographic Origin - Asian applicants dominate at $66.2\%$, followed by Europe ($14.6\%$) and North America ($12.9\%$)
  • Education Levels - $78.0\%$ hold advanced degrees—predominantly Bachelor's ($40.2\%$) and Master's ($37.8\%$)—over Doctorate ($8.6\%$) and High School ($13.4\%$).
  • Work Experience & Training - $58.1\%$ possess prior experience, while $88.4\%$ require no job training, pointing to a highly job-ready candidate pool.
  • Geographic Demand - Role placements cluster heavily across three U.S. regions: Northeast ($28.2\%$), South ($27.5\%$), and West ($25.8\%$).
  • Role Permanence - $89.4\%$ of positions are full-time, with $90.1\%$ using annual salary metrics (year), indicating long-term employment sponsorship over temporary contracts.
  • Approval Rate - Target variable baseline yields a $66.8\%$ certification rate vs. a $33.2\%$ denial rate (approx. 2:1 ratio).

Categorical features and target variables using Crosstab¶

In [22]:
# define list of categorical features to plot countplot for analysis
cat_features = ['continent', 'education_of_employee', 'has_job_experience', 'requires_job_training', 'region_of_employment', 'unit_of_wage', 'full_time_position', 'case_status']
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 12))


# plotting the boxplots for each numerical feature with percentage in the bars
for i, feature in enumerate(cat_features):
  plt.subplot(3,3,i+1)

  # create crosstab for case_status vs category feature
  tab = pd.crosstab(data[feature], data['case_status'], normalize='index')

  # plot within current subplt (ax passed explicitly),
  # creating a stacked bar chart from the normalized crosstab
  tab.plot(kind='bar', stacked=True, ax=plt.gca())
  plt.title(f'Crosstab of {feature} vs case_status')
  plt.xlabel(feature)
  plt.ylabel('Percentage')

  # adding a legend for the 'case_status' column
  plt.legend(title='case_status', labels=['Denied', 'Certified'])

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations¶

  • Continent - Certification rates remain generally high across origins, peaking with Europe, followed sequentially by Africa, Asia, North America, and Oceania.
  • Education - Advanced degree holders (Doctorate and Master’s) achieve higher certification likelihoods compared to Bachelor’s and High School candidates.
  • Job Experience - Candidates with prior work experience exhibit a moderately higher certification rate than non-experienced applicants.
  • Requires Job Training - Certification-to-denial ratios are virtually identical across both classes, indicating negligible feature importance.
  • Region of Employment - Approval rates peak in the Midwest, followed by the South, Northeast, and West, with Island locations yielding the lowest success rates.
  • Unit of Wage - Year-based compensation shows the highest certification success (around 75%), however hourly roles drop sharply to the lowest approval tier of 35% to 40%
  • Full-Time Position - Full-time and non-full-time indicators demonstrate nearly identical class distributions, offering limited predictive signal.

Summary¶

  • Key Discriminators - Candidate education level and wage unit structure yield the strongest feature importance for predicting visa certification outcomes.
  • Non-Predictive Attributes - Job training requirements and full-time employment status offer negligible signal, demonstrating virtually no influence on certification class separation.

Outlier Detection and treatment¶

In [26]:
# outlier detection using boxplot
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 7))

# define the list of continuous numerical features to plot boxplot to analyse the distribution and its skewness
numerical_features = ['no_of_employees', 'prevailing_wage', 'yr_of_estab']

for i, var in enumerate(numerical_features):
    plt.subplot(3, 3, i+1)
    sns.boxplot(data[var])
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.title(f'Distribution of {var}')



plt.show()

Observations¶

  • no_of_employees - Extreme upper-tail outliers (>600k) and invalid negative entries (e.g., -26) require aggressive data cleaning, capping, or imputation prior to modeling.
  • prevailing_wage - Significant upper-bound dispersion (>300k) reflects valid high-income roles rather than noise; standardizing values to a unified annual scale based on unit_of_wage is essential before applying transformations.
  • yr_of_estab - Far-left tail values representing founding dates prior to 1900 act as leverage points and should be handled via floor capping or binning.

Observations¶

  • Data Anomaly Identification - The negative no_of_employees entry reflects a localized data entry error rather than an invalid record, as all associated applicant attributes are valid and well-distributed.
  • Imputation Strategy - Impute invalid employee values using the median - a robust measure of central tendency resilient to severe right-tail dispersion.
  • Data Leakage Prevention - Compute and fit median imputations strictly on the training partition after the train-test split to prevent target and data leakage.

Treatment of yr_of_estab outliers¶

  • Rather than dropping records predating 1900 - which risks critical data loss * Transform yr_of_estab into a continuous company_age metric calculated against the dataset reference year (company_age = 2026 - yr_of_estab).
  • Engineering company_age provides numerical continuity, rescales historical temporal gaps, and exposes a standardized feature representation that ML algorithms optimize more effectively.

Treatment of prevailing_wage outliers¶

  • prevailing_wage is intrinsically tied to unit_of_wage. EDA reveals that class separation is driven primarily by the temporal unit rather than the absolute wage amount.
  • The extreme dispersion in wage data (mean - 74k, std - 52k and ranges from \$2.13 to \$319,210) stems directly from mixed reporting scales. Comparing unstandardized metrics (e.g., weekly vs. annual) introduces severe scale distortion that degrades algorithm performance.
  • Given the inherent lack of mathematical comparability without complex normalization and its weak standalone predictive signal - prevailing_wage will be dropped from the modeling pipeline.

Observations¶

  • Yearly Wages - High variance with extensive upper outliers (>$200000) and a median lower than monthly or weekly categories.
  • Monthly & Weekly Wages - Elevated median wage baselines compared to annual terms (skewed by lower sample sizes), with upper outliers stretching to \$250000.
  • Hourly Wages - Compact distribution centered at the lowest overall compensation level with virtually no outliers.

Consideration¶

  • Standardizing wages across units via heuristic conversions (e.g., assuming 8-hour days, 5-day weeks, 52-week years) risks compounding extreme outlier distortion.

Conclusion¶

  • Due to structural scaling inconsistencies and potential noise amplification, prevailing_wage will be dropped from the modeling pipeline.

# Replace negative values with np.nan

# Impute the missing values with SimpleImputer
imp_median = SimpleImputer(missing_values=np.nan, strategy='median')

# fit the imputer on train data and transform the train data

# transform the validation and test data using the imputer fit on train data
X_val['no_of_employees'] = imp_median.transform(X_val[['no_of_employees']])
X_test['no_of_employees'] = imp_median.transform(X_test[['no_of_employees']])

Model Building - Original Data¶

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

what does OFLC want?¶

  • A reliable classification model to predict VISA approval outcomes.
  • Insights into key decision factors that influence approvals/denials

Reference from the problem statement : Recommend a suitable profile for the applicants for whom the visa should be certified or denied based on the drivers that significantly influence the case status.

Where can the model go wrong?¶

  • False Positives : Predicting a Visa will be approved when it gets denied in reality could mislead employers and waste their resources.
  • False Negatives : Predicting a Visa will be denied when it gets approved in reality may unfairly reject strong candidates.

Which case is more important?¶

False Positives are more important to minimize, as predicting visa appoval for candidates who ultimately get denied can:

  • Mislead employers into investing time and resources in unqualified candidates.
  • Undermine the credibility and efficiency of the visa processing system.
  • This could also lead to challenges like non-compliance with regulations.

False Negatives are tolerable (but worth monitoring) as EasyVisa could reject someone who could have been approved.

Which metric to optimize?¶

Metrics to optimise in order

  1. Precision: Focuses on minimizing False Positives. High precision = OFLC reviews mostly truly certifiable cases.
  2. F1-Score: Balances precision and recall; useful to ensure resonable overall performance.
  3. Recall : Important, but secondary - we can afford to miss a few good cases if it helps reduce OFLC's load.

How to reduce the losses?¶

  • Use robust feature engineering and ensemble models(eg: AdaBoost, GradeintBoost, XGBoost, Bagging, Random Forest).
  • Apply class imbalance handling (SMOTE, Random Under Sampling, class weights).
  • Use hyper parameter tuning techniques.

Utility Functions¶

In [44]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model build using sklearn
def model_performance_classification(model, predictors, target):
  """
  Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

  model: classifier
  predictors: independent variables
  target: dependent variable
  """

  # predicting using the independent variables
  pred = model.predict(predictors)

  acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)
  recall = recall_score(target, pred)
  precision = precision_score(target, pred)
  f1 = f1_score(target, pred)

  # creating a dataframe of metrics
  df_perf = pd.DataFrame({
      'Accuracy': acc,
      'Recall': recall,
      'Precision': precision,
      'F1': f1,
      }, index=[0])

  return df_perf
In [45]:
# function to create a single DataFrame of training, validation performances
def model_performances(train, validation):

  # combine the dataframes across rows
  combined = pd.concat([train, validation], axis=0, keys=["Training", "Validation"])

  # drop the index
  combined.reset_index(level=1, drop=True)
  return combined
In [46]:
# function to plot the confusion matrix of training and validation, side by side
def plot_confusion_matrices_v2(model, training_predictors, training_target, validation_predictors, validation_target, validation_label = 'Validation Confusion Matrix'):

  """
  Function to plot the confusion matrix of training and validation datasets.
  model: trained classifier
  training_predictors: independent variables for training data
  training_target: dependent variable for training data
  validation_predict
  """

  def compute_cm_labels(cm):
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            f"{item}\n{item/cm.sum():.2%}"
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2,2)
    return labels

  # Predict on training and validation data
  y_train_pred = model.predict(training_predictors)
  y_val_pred = model.predict(validation_predictors)

  # Compute confusion matrices
  cm_train = confusion_matrix(training_target, y_train_pred)
  cm_val = confusion_matrix(validation_target, y_val_pred)

  # Compute labels for confusion matrices
  labels_train = compute_cm_labels(cm_train)
  labels_val = compute_cm_labels(cm_val)

  # Plot side-by-side
  fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6))
  sns.heatmap(cm_train, annot=labels_train, fmt='', ax=axes[0])
  axes[0].set_title('Training Confusion Matrix')
  axes[0].set_xlabel('Predicted Labels')
  axes[0].set_ylabel('True Labels')

  sns.heatmap(cm_val, annot=labels_val, fmt='', ax=axes[1])
  axes[1].set_title(validation_label)
  axes[1].set_xlabel('Predicted Labels')
  axes[1].set_ylabel('True Labels')

  plt.tight_layout()
  plt.show()

# function to create the dataframe comparing original and sampled data
def create_sample_comparison(predictor, validator, predictor_sampled, validator_sampled):
  sampled_data_frame = {
      'Label 1 Count' : [
          sum(validator ==1),
          sum(validator_sampled ==1)
      ],
      'Label 0 Count' : [
          sum(validator ==0),
          sum(validator_sampled ==0)
      ],
      'X Shape' : [
          predictor.shape,
          predictor_sampled.shape
      ],
      'Y Shape' : [
          validator.shape,
          validator_sampled.shape
      ]
  }

  # Create the DataFrame with appropriate index labels
  df_summary = pd.DataFrame(sampled_data_frame, index=['Before Sampling', 'After Sampling'])

  return df_summary

  • Evaluation Framework - Performance will be assessed across Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score, with F1 Score designated as the primary metric to optimize the precision-recall trade-off.

  • No hyper parameters will be provided

Model Observation Summary¶

  • A near-perfect training F1 score of 0.999 demonstrates that the model is memorizing training noise rather than capturing true underlying patterns.
  • The validation F1 score drops sharply to 0.527, highlighting a severe performance gap between train and holdout datasets.
  • Validation precision stands at 0.567, reflecting only moderate accuracy when classifying positive visa certification outcomes.
  • The substantial disparity between training and validation metrics confirms significant variance and unmitigated overfitting.
  • While Random Forest marginally outperforms the standard Bagging Classifier on validation data, both ensemble models continue to suffer from persistent overfitting.

Model Building - Oversampled Data¶

  • Training data will be oversampled for the above models using SMOTE
  • The model trained on oversampled data will be validated against the validation dataset

Oversample data using SMOTE¶

In [66]:
# Fit SMOTE on train data (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique)
# Sample the minority 'Certified' Class to 0.67
smote = SMOTE(sampling_strategy=0.67, random_state=1)
X_train_over, y_train_over = smote.fit_resample(X_train, y_train)

Hyperparameter Tuning¶

Candidate Selection: The top 3 performing models will be selected from an evaluation matrix of 18 total configurations (6 core modeling techniques evaluated across 3 sampling regimes: baseline original, oversampled, and undersampled).

Evaluated Algorithms:

  1. Decision Tree Classifier
  2. Bagging Classifier
  3. Random Forest Classifier
  4. AdaBoost Classifier
  5. Gradient Boosting Classifier
  6. XGBoost Classifier

Selection of Top 3 Models for hyper-parameter tuning¶

Gradient Boost (Oversampled)

  • A precision score of 0.6394 ranks among the highest evaluated, directly advancing the core objective of minimizing false-positive misclassifications.
  • An F1 score of 0.5846 establishes a robust balance between decision precision and minority instance detection.
  • A recall rate of 0.5384 provides sufficient sensitivity to prevent excessive false negatives on minority class predictions.
  • The pipeline effectively mitigates class imbalance by leveraging the combined strengths of synthetic oversampling and gradient boosting dynamics.

XGBoost (Oversampled)

  • A competitive precision score of 0.6160 demonstrates consistent decision confidence across model variations.
  • An F1 score of 0.5555 maintains a reliable equilibrium between overall accuracy and sensitivity.
  • A recall rate of 0.5059 delivers above-average minority detection relative to comparable high-precision candidates.
  • Robust structural stability makes this model architecture highly scalable for complex, high-volume production deployments.

AdaBoost (Oversampled)

  • A precision score of 0.6411 closely rivals Gradient Boosting, effectively minimizing false-positive misclassifications and incorrect visa certifications.
  • An F1 score of 0.5387 provides a solid trade-off, outperforming simpler AdaBoost variants.
  • A recall rate of 0.4645 remains acceptable given the model's strong emphasis on high precision.
  • Structural simplicity and fast training times make this architecture well-suited for low-latency, early-stage production deployments.

Why Undersampled Models were not choosen¶

  • Precision-Recall Trade-Off - Despite achieving elevated recall (>= 0.70), undersampled models exhibit reduced precision (e.g., 0.52 for undersampled XGBoost), which increases the rate of false-positive misclassifications.
  • Metric Degradation - Although overall F1 scores remain reasonable, they underperform relative to their synthetic oversampling counterparts.
  • Information Loss - Discarding majority class data during undersampling risks weakening overall model generalization, potentially causing the pipeline to miss valid, approval-worthy cases.

Why Simple Models were not choosen¶

  • High Variance & Overfitting - Unbalanced simple architectures (e.g., standard Decision Trees, Bagging, and AdaBoost) exhibit severe high variance, marked by near-perfect training metrics contrasted against weak validation precision.
  • Depressed Metric Balance - Overall F1 scores remain constrained in the 0.48 - 0.55 range, highlighting a poor trade-off between precision and recall.
  • Sensitivity to Imbalance - Lacking explicit sampling techniques, these models fail to adequately learn minority class patterns.
  • Production Vulnerability - Limited structural resilience makes these simpler baselines susceptible to data drift and performance degradation under real-world variance.

1. Tuning AdaBoost (Oversampled)¶

Hyper Parameters¶

Below hyper parameters will be used for AdaBoost tuning

  • base_estimator - The underlying base learner from which the boosted ensemble is built (defaults to a Decision Tree with max_depth=1).
  • n_estimators - The maximum number of weak learners constructed before boosting terminates (defaults to 50).
  • learning_rate - The shrinkage factor applied to adjust each classifier's contribution, governing a direct trade-off with n_estimators.

Cross Validation¶

For cross validation GridSearchCV will be used

  • scoring will be done for precision and F1 score
  • To parallelise n_jobs=-1 will be used
In [107]:
# Grid of parameters to choose from
ada_parameters = {
    # Different max_depth for estimator
    "estimator": [DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=1), DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=1), DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=1)],
    "n_estimators": [100, 200, 300, 400],
    "learning_rate": [0.1, 0.2]
}

# Precision and F1 scoring used to compare parameter combinations
ada_scoring = {
    'precision': metrics.make_scorer(metrics.precision_score),
    'f1': metrics.make_scorer(metrics.f1_score)
}

# Create and run the grid search for all above combinations of hyper parameters
# Use ada_boost_classifier_over model
ada_grid_search = GridSearchCV(ada_boost_classifier_oversampled, ada_parameters, scoring=ada_scoring, refit='f1', cv=5, n_jobs=-1)
ada_grid_search = ada_grid_search.fit(X_train_over, y_train_over)

# Set the clf to the best combination of parameters
ada_boost_classifier_tuned = ada_grid_search.best_estimator_

# Fit the best algorithm to the data.
ada_boost_classifier_tuned.fit(X_train_over, y_train_over)

3. Tuning XG Boost (Oversampled)¶

Hyper Parameters¶

Following XGBoost hyper parameters will be used to tune to increase the model performance.

  • n_estimators - The total number of trees the model will build. More trees can capture more patterns, but take longer to train.
  • scale_pos_weight - Controls the balance between positive and negative data. This is useful when one outcome (like visa fraud) is very rare, helping the model pay attention to it.
  • subsample - The percentage of training data randomly picked to build each tree. Using a fraction instead of all data helps prevent the model from memorizing the answers.
  • learning_rate - Controls how fast the model learns. A smaller learning rate makes the model more cautious and stable, though it requires more trees.
  • gamma - The minimum amount of error reduction needed to make a new split in a tree. Higher values stop the model from making unnecessary, overly complex splits.
  • colsample_bytree - The percentage of features (columns) randomly chosen for each tree. This adds variety and prevents the model from relying too much on a single feature.
  • colsample_bylevel - The percentage of features randomly chosen at each specific level (depth) as the tree grows downward.
  • max_depth - The maximum number of splits deep each tree can grow. Deeper trees learn more complex rules, but risk overfitting the training data.

Cross Validation¶

An automated search tool that tests multiple combinations of your XGBoost hyperparameters to find the best-performing set using cross-validation.

  • Precision and F1 Score - The scoring metrics used to evaluate the model. Precision ensures that when the model approves or flags an application, it is usually correct. The F1 score balances precision and recall, making it ideal when dealing with rare outcomes.
  • n_jobs=-1 - A setting that tells your computer to use all available CPU cores simultaneously, speeding up the search process significantly.
In [115]:
# Grid of hyper parameters to choose from GridSearchCV using XG Boost
xgb_parameters = {
    "n_estimators":[100, 150, 200],
    "learning_rate":[0.1,0.2],
    "subsample":[0.6,0.7,0.9,1],
    "gamma":[0,0.5,1],
    "colsample_bytree":[0.7,0.9,1],
    "colsample_bylevel":[0.7,0.9,1],
    "max_depth":[3,4,5]
}

# Precision and F1 scoring used to compare parameter combinations
xgb_scoring = {
    'precision': metrics.make_scorer(metrics.precision_score),
    'f1': metrics.make_scorer(metrics.f1_score)
}

# Create and run the grid search for all above combinations of hyper parameters
xgb_grid_search = GridSearchCV(xg_boost_classifier_oversampled, xgb_parameters, scoring=xgb_scoring, refit='f1', cv=5, n_jobs=-1)
xgb_grid_search = xgb_grid_search.fit(X_train_over, y_train_over)

# Set the clf to the best combination of parameters
xg_boost_classifier_tuned = xgb_grid_search.best_estimator_

# Fit the best algorithm to the data.
xg_boost_classifier_tuned.fit(X_train_over, y_train_over)

Observations on hyperparameter models¶

Here are the performance results for the three hyperparameter-tuned, oversampled models (AdaBoost, GradientBoost, and XGBoost)

1. Best Precision (Validation Set) :¶

  • GradientBoost : 0.642408
  • XGBoost : 0.642349
  • AdaBoost : 0.629975

Key Observation : Precision is the important metric for EasyVisa, and GradientBoost performs best in our case.

2. Best F1 Score (Validation Set) :¶

  • AdaBoost : 0.586982
  • XGBoost : 0.582728
  • GradientBoost : 0.579651

Key Observation : F1 Score is the next important metric (Precision-recall balance), and AdaBoost slightly edges out the other.

3. Recall (Balance Check) :¶

  • AdaBoost : 0.549483
  • XGBoost : 0.533235
  • GradientBoost : 0.528065

Key Observation : AdaBoost maintains reasonable recall while optimizing precision.

4. Robustness to Overfitting (Gap Analysis) :¶

Training vs Validation F1 gap:

  • AdaBoost : 0.686178 - 0.586982 (Gap : 0.099196)
  • XGBoost : 0.697671 - 0.582728 (Gap : 0.114943)
  • GradientBoost : 0.690991 - 0.579651 (Gap : 0.11134)

Key Observation : All models generalize similarly well, But AdaBoost having lesser gap than other models.

5. Higher Baseline Across Metrics (Training) :¶

  • AdaBoost achieved superior recall and F1 scores with good precision across both training and validation, indicating a better-optimized learing fit.

Recommended Final Model for testing¶

  • AdaBoost (Hyperparameter Tuned) and is selected based on the below key factors
  1. Achieved the highest Recall and F1 with good precision scores on the validation set, matching the primary optimization goals.
  2. Balanced performance without signs of overfitting.
  3. Slight but consistent edge in performance over both GradientBoost and AdaBoost.

Model Performance summary on Test Data¶

  • The test F1 score (0.601) stays relatively close to the training F1 score (0.686), showing that the model transfers well to unseen data.
  • A test precision score of 0.655 indicates that the model is effective at minimizing false positives
  • Recall decreases moderately from 0.637 to 0.556 on the test set, meaning the model misses a portion of actual positive cases.
  • The model demonstrates reliable generalization overall and maintains a strong focus on precision.

Actionable Insights & Recommendations¶

Key Highlights : Business Recommendations¶

  • Prioritize Job Experience: Focus evaluation on applicant work history as a primary success indicator.

  • Filter by Education: Implement strategic screening based on high-school or qualification levels.

  • Target Regional Demographics: Focus on Asian applicant profiles within specific US target regions.

  • Target Yearly Wages: Favor positions offering annual salaries, which correlate with higher approval rates.

  • Exclude Low-Impact Factors: Streamline processing by dropping features that contribute little predictive value.

  • Deploy for Workload Reduction: Integrate the model to automate and reduce manual OFLC review volumes.

Detailed : Business Recommendations¶

1. Prioritize Job Experience

  • Use work history as a primary positive screening filter for high-probability candidates.
  • Strongly favor applicants with prior experience, as it stands as the second-highest predictor (0.15 importance) of visa approval.
  • Filter out or lower the priority for candidates lacking work experience, as they show significantly lower approval rates.

2. Filter by Education

  • Recommend Bachelor's and Master's degree holders for positive outcomes, as they historically show higher approval rates.
  • Allocate moderate priority to Doctorate candidates while focusing primary resources on Bachelor's and Master's applicants.
  • Use High School education as a negative screening filter, given its high model importance (0.24) pointing toward rejection patterns.

3. Target Regional Demographics

  • Focus recruitment and screening on Asian candidates, who show a strong positive correlation (0.06 importance) with approvals.
  • Direct more resources toward processing Asian applicant profiles to maximize approval success rates.
  • Prioritize applications originating from the West, South, and Northeast regions, which demonstrate moderate predictive importance.

4. Target Yearly Wages

  • Focus on applications with annual salary structures rather than hourly or weekly positions, given their higher predictive importance ($0.07$).
  • Treat yearly wages as a positive signal for stable, full-time roles that align with OFLC approval criteria.
  • Deprioritize or filter out lower-commitment hourly positions to improve overall approval probability.

5. Exclude Low-Impact Factors

  • Exclude company size and company age from primary screening criteria due to their minimal predictive power.
  • Streamline application evaluations by focusing exclusively on high-importance features.
  • Reduce screening complexity to enable faster and more efficient candidate processing.

6. Deploy for Workload Reduction

  • Deploy the 67% precision model to pre-filter applications and reduce the manual OFLC review burden by approximately 33%.
  • Apply a structured workflow combining automated filtering with manual reviews specifically for edge cases.
  • Accept the 54% recall constraint while efficiently capturing the majority of approvable candidates.
  • Continuously track model performance and refine thresholds based on OFLC feedback and real-world approval outcomes.

Model Limitations and Business Considerations¶

Model Interpretability and Trust:

  • Maintain transparency with OFLC stakeholders regarding key decision factors (education, experience, geography) and use the model as a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for human reviewers, particularly for complex cases.

Bias and Fairness Concerns:

  • Mitigate historical OFLC decision biases that may unfairly impact specific groups, ensure compliance with labor fairness laws, and conduct regular audits to maintain equitable treatment.

Precision-Recall Trade-offs:

  • Balance the 67% precision focus (which reduces false approvals but risks rejecting qualified candidates) against the 54% recall limitation, ensuring threshold flexibility aligns with agency capacity and priorities.

Ongoing Maintenance and Data Quality:

  • Retrain the model every 6 to 12 months to adapt to evolving policies, establish feedback loops for incorrectly rejected applications, and address data inconsistencies like prevailing wage outliers and missing context.
